[notes-n1] Notes 1. Columns in a frame
A column carries the floors above it down to the foundation. Its axial load grows storey by storey from the roof down, and it also takes moments: from its continuity with the beams when the spans or the loads on either side differ, from sway when wind pushes on a frame without bracing, and from the small eccentricity that EC2 assumes for every compression member. Every column design starts with one question: is the column short (non-slender) or slender? The answer decides whether the design for N and M in Unit 8 is enough, or whether the second-order moment of Unit 9 must be added.
Column (EC2 5.3.1(7)) A member whose section depth does not exceed 4 times its width (h ≤ 4b) and whose height is at least 3 times its section depth. A longer, thinner section is designed as a wall.
[Figure: A short column fails when its section crushes. A slender column bends sideways first: the deflection e gives the load a lever arm, the extra moment N·e increases the deflection, and the column fails at a lower load.]
The design of a column follows nine steps (course notes). This Unit is step 6; Unit 8 covers steps 7 to 9 for a short column, and Unit 9 adds the second-order moment for a slender one.
Step Task Reference Unit
1–2 Design life, exposure, fire resistance; materials EN 1990 Table 2.1; EC2 Table 4.1 RCD I
3–4 Column size for fire; cover for durability, fire and bond EN 1992-1-2 Table 5.2a; EC2 4.4.1 8
5 Axial force and moments from the analysis EC2 Section 5 3–6, 8
6 Classify: braced or unbraced, short or slender EC2 5.8.3 7
7 Design moment (with the second-order moment if slender) EC2 5.8.8 8, 9
8–9 Longitudinal bars from the N–M interaction; links and detailing EC2 6.1; 9.5 8
Key points:
- EC2 column: h ≤ 4b and a height of at least 3h; otherwise a wall.
- A column carries axial load and moment: continuity, sway and a minimum eccentricity.
- Short columns crush; slender columns bend sideways first, and N·e adds moment.
Quick check (not graded): Each member below is 3.0 m high. Which one does EC2 5.3.1(7) treat as a wall rather than a column?
Options: 300 × 300 mm | 250 × 800 mm | 200 × 1000 mm | 400 × 600 mm
Explanation shown after answering: 1000/200 = 5 > 4, so the 200 × 1000 section is a wall. The 250 × 800 section (3.2) is still a column. All four are tall enough: 3.0 m ≥ 3h needs h ≤ 1000 mm.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. Braced or unbraced, short or slender
A column is braced when walls, a lift core or bracing carry all the horizontal load of the building, so its ends cannot move sideways relative to each other. It is unbraced when the frame itself resists the horizontal load by bending of its columns and beams: the column sways. The project frame you analysed for wind in Units 5 and 6 has no walls or cores, so its columns are unbraced.
[Figure: Braced: the shear wall takes the wind and the column ends stay in line. Unbraced: the frame sways by Δ and every column bends to resist it.]
Braced and bracing members (EC2 5.8.1) Bracing members (walls, cores) are assumed to contribute to the overall horizontal stability of the structure. Braced members are assumed not to contribute to it, so they are designed without sway.
Any column deflects a little under load, and the axial load acting on that deflection adds a moment: the second-order effect . EC2 5.8.2(6) lets you ignore it when it is less than 10% of the first-order effects, and 5.8.3.1 turns that into a simple test: compare the slenderness λ with a limit λ_{lim} (§5 and §6). Below the limit the column is non-slender (short); above it the column is slender .
Non-slender (λ ≤ λ_{lim}) Slender (λ > λ_{lim})
Braced M_{Ed} from the first-order moments (Unit 8) Add M_2 near mid-height (Unit 9)
Unbraced As braced, with the sway moments (rare: λ_{lim} is low) Add M_2 at the ends (Unit 9)
Key points:
- Braced: walls or cores take the horizontal load; the column does not sway. Unbraced: the frame sways.
- Second-order effect: N times the deflection. Ignore it only if λ ≤ λ_{lim}.
- Classify each column twice: braced or unbraced, then short or slender, about each axis.
Quick check (not graded): A four-storey office block has a reinforced concrete lift core and two shear walls that carry all the wind load. Its interior columns are
Options: unbraced, because the building is four storeys high | braced, because the core and walls take the horizontal load | slender, because every column in a building is slender | bracing members
Explanation shown after answering: The core and the walls are the bracing members; the columns are braced, so they carry no sway. Whether they are slender is a separate question, answered with λ and λ_{lim}.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. Effective length
Press the ends of a long ruler together and it bows sideways at a small force; a ruler half as long needs about four times the force. Euler’s buckling load explains why: it falls with the square of the length.
EQUATION (7.1): N_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{l_0^{\,2}}
Effective length l_0 (EC2 5.8.1) The length of a pin-ended column with the same section and the same buckling load as the real one. On the buckled shape it is the distance between two points of zero moment (points of contraflexure).
[Figure: Ideal end conditions and their effective lengths (after EC2 Figure 5.7). Real columns in frames sit between the ideal cases: braced, 0.5l ≤ l_0 ≤ l; unbraced, l_0 ≥ l.]
- l is the clear height between the end restraints: in this course, the storey height minus the depth of the beams framing in the plane considered (the deeper one where two differ).
- Fixing an end against rotation shortens l_0: the buckled shape curves back, and the points of contraflexure move inside the column.
- Letting an end sway lengthens l_0: a column fixed at the base and free at the top buckles like half of a pin-ended column twice as long.
- Beams give partial restraint: neither fixed nor pinned. §4 measures how much.
Key points:
- N_{cr} = π²EI/l_0²: half the effective length, four times the buckling load.
- Ideal cases: l, 2l, 0.7l, 0.5l, and l for fixed ends that sway.
- l is the clear height; braced 0.5l ≤ l_0 ≤ l, unbraced l_0 ≥ l.
Quick check (not graded): Four columns have the same section and the same clear height l. Which has the lowest buckling load?
Options: Pinned at both ends | Fixed at the base, free at the top | Fixed at the base, pinned at the top | Fixed at both ends
Explanation shown after answering: The free top lets it sway: l_0 = 2l, the longest of the four, so N_{cr} is a quarter of the pin-ended value and one sixteenth of the value for fixed ends (l_0 = 0.5l).

[notes-n4] Notes 4. Effective length from the beams
For a column in a regular frame, EC2 5.8.3.2(3) gives l_0 from the clear height l and the relative flexibilities k_1 and k_2 of the restraints at the bottom and top ends.
EQUATION (7.2): \text{Braced:}\quad l_0 = 0.5\,l\sqrt{\left(1+\frac{k_1}{0.45+k_1}\right)\left(1+\frac{k_2}{0.45+k_2}\right)}
EQUATION (7.3): \text{Unbraced:}\quad l_0 = l\cdot\max\left\{\sqrt{1+10\,\frac{k_1 k_2}{k_1+k_2}}\;;\;\left(1+\frac{k_1}{1+k_1}\right)\left(1+\frac{k_2}{1+k_2}\right)\right\}
EC2 defines k = (θ/M)(EI/l): the rotation of the restraining members per unit moment, scaled by the column’s own stiffness. The course method (RDF §14, Mosley §9.2) evaluates it as a ratio of stiffnesses at each end:
EQUATION (7.4): k = \frac{(I/l)_{\mathrm{column}}}{\sum 2\,(I/l)_{\mathrm{beam}}} \;\ge\; 0.1
[Figure: Each axis has its own clear height and its own beams: the beams that bend with the column in that plane. Bending about z uses I_z = bh³/12 and the main beams; bending about y uses I_y = hb³/12 and the secondary beams.]
- Each beam counts as 2EI/l, a reduced stiffness that allows for cracking in the beams (RDF note 2; EC2 5.8.3.2(5)). E cancels, so I/l is enough.
- The columns above and below are ignored (RDF note 2). Where an adjacent column is likely to buckle with this one and rotate the joint, EC2 5.8.3.2(4) adds its EI/l to the column term, which raises k.
- k = 0 means a rigid restraint and k = ∞ means none. Fully rigid restraint is rare, so EC2 recommends k ≥ 0.1. A column fixed into a footing designed for the moment takes k_1 = 0.1; a pinned end takes k = ∞, which makes its bracket in (7.2) equal 2.
- A beam on one side only, as at an edge or corner column, gives a larger k: one stiffness in the sum instead of two.
k_1 = k_2 = k 0.1 0.25 0.5 1.0 ∞
Braced, l_0/l (7.2) 0.59 0.68 0.76 0.84 1.00
Unbraced, l_0/l (7.3) 1.22 1.50 1.87 2.45 ∞
Stiffer beams (smaller k) give a shorter l_0. With k at its floor of 0.1, a braced column has l_0 = 0.59l and an unbraced one 1.22l: the same column and beams give twice the effective length once the frame can sway.
Worked line: course notes Example 1, about z Column 275 × 350, storey 5.0 m, main beams 250 × 500 at 6 m and 8 m on both floors: l = 5000 − 500 = 4500 mm; K_c = (275 × 350³/12)/4500 = 2.183 × 10⁵ mm³; ΣK_b = 4.340 + 3.255 = 7.595 × 10⁵ mm³; k = 2.183/(2 × 7.595) = 0.1437 at both ends; l_0 = 0.5 × 4500 × (1 + 0.1437/0.5937) = 2795 mm. The notes print b × h = 275 × 300 in one line; the section is 275 × 350, as the figure and every number show.
Key points:
- Braced (7.2), unbraced (7.3): take the larger of the two terms for an unbraced column.
- k = (I/l)_{col}/Σ2(I/l)_{beam} at each end, never below 0.1; fixed base k_1 = 0.1, pinned end k = ∞.
- Each axis uses its own clear height and the beams that bend in its plane.
Quick check (not graded): For a braced column between deep beams, (I/l)_{col}/Σ2(I/l)_{beam} = 0.06 at both ends. Which effective length do you use?
Options: 0.50 l | 0.56 l | 0.59 l | 0.75 l
Explanation shown after answering: k is raised to its floor of 0.1, so l_0 = 0.5l(1 + 0.1/0.55) = 0.59l. With k = 0.06 you would get 0.56l, a column restrained more rigidly than EC2 accepts; 0.75l is the BS 8110 table value of §5.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. The slenderness ratio
EQUATION (7.5): \lambda = \frac{l_0}{i}, \qquad i = \sqrt{\frac{I}{A}}
EQUATION (7.6): \text{Rectangle:}\quad i = \frac{h}{\sqrt{12}} = 0.289\,h \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \lambda \approx 3.46\,\frac{l_0}{h}
- i is the radius of gyration of the uncracked concrete section about the axis of bending; h is the side in the plane of bending, square to that axis.
- Check both axes. About the minor axis i is smaller, so λ is usually larger there, but l_0 can differ between the axes because the beams differ.
- Course notes Example 1: i_z = 350/√12 = 101.0 mm and λ_z = 2795/101.0 = 27.7; i_y = 275/√12 = 79.4 mm and λ_y = 2718/79.4 = 34.2.
The simplified method of the course notes The notes also give l_0 = β × clear height from BS 8110 Tables 3.19 (braced: β = 0.75 to 1.0) and 3.20 (unbraced: β = 1.2 to 2.2), with end conditions 1 to 4. It is a quick estimate from a withdrawn code, and for columns between stiff beams it gives a longer l_0 than (7.2): in Example 1, 0.75 × 4600 = 3450 mm makes λ_y = 43.5 and the column slender about y, where (7.2) gives 2718 mm and non-slender. This course designs with (7.2) and (7.3) and uses the tables as a cross-check.
Key points:
- λ = l_0/i; for a rectangle i = h/√12, with h in the plane of bending.
- Estimate first: λ ≈ 3.5 l_0/h.
- BS 8110 β-tables: a cross-check only; design with (7.2) and (7.3).
Quick check (not graded): A braced 250 × 500 column has l_0 = 3.0 m about both axes. Which statement is right?
Options: λ = 20.8 about both axes | λ = 41.6 about the minor axis and 20.8 about the major axis | λ = 41.6 about the major axis | λ = 12.0 about the minor axis
Explanation shown after answering: i = 250/√12 = 72.2 mm about the minor axis, so λ = 3000/72.2 = 41.6; about the major axis i = 500/√12 = 144.3 mm and λ = 20.8. The value 12.0 is l_0/h, which forgets the √12.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. The slenderness limit
EC2 5.8.3.1 sets the slenderness below which second-order effects may be ignored. It depends on the creep, the steel, the shape of the moment diagram and, above all, on how hard the column is pushed.
EQUATION (7.7): \lambda_{lim} = \frac{20\,A\,B\,C}{\sqrt{n}}
EQUATION (7.8): A = \frac{1}{1+0.2\,\varphi_{ef}}\;(0.7),\qquad B = \sqrt{1+2\omega}\;(1.1),\qquad C = 1.7 - r_m
EQUATION (7.9): n = \frac{N_{Ed}}{A_c\,f_{cd}}, \quad f_{cd} = \frac{0.85\,f_{ck}}{1.5} = 0.567\,f_{ck}, \qquad r_m = \frac{M_{01}}{M_{02}},\;\; |M_{02}| \ge |M_{01}|
- A = 0.7 and B = 1.1 when the effective creep ratio φ_{ef} and the steel ratio ω = A_sf_{yd}/(A_cf_{cd}) are not yet known, as when you size a column. Calculate C wherever you can: it has the largest effect.
- n is the relative axial force. A column carrying more load has a lower limit: double n and λ_{lim} falls by 29%.
[Figure: The sign of r_m. Single curvature bulges the column most and gives the lowest limit; double curvature keeps the deflection small and raises the limit.]
Case r_m C
Single curvature: M_{01} and M_{02} give tension on the same face 0 to +1 1.7 down to 0.7
Double curvature: tension on opposite faces 0 to −1 1.7 up to 2.7
Braced, moments only or mainly from imperfections or transverse load: in this course, when |M_{02}| ≤ N_{Ed}l_0/400, or there are no end moments 1.0 0.7
Unbraced, in general 1.0 0.7
Then compare, about each axis separately (EC2 5.8.3.1(2)): λ ≤ λ_{lim} means non-slender, and the column is designed for its first-order moments with the minimum eccentricity (Unit 8); λ > λ_{lim} means slender, and the second-order moment M_2 is added (Unit 9). Course notes Example 1: n = 1050 × 10³/(275 × 350 × 14.17) = 0.770; about z, r_m = −12/40 = −0.30, C = 2.00 and λ_{lim} = 20 × 0.7 × 1.1 × 2.00/√0.770 = 35.1 > 27.7; about y, r_m = −10/15 = −0.667, C = 2.367 and λ_{lim} = 41.5 > 34.2. Non-slender about both axes.
Two slips to avoid RDF §14 prints |M_{02}| ≤ |M_{01}|; EC2 has |M_{02}| ≥ |M_{01}|, so M_{02} is always the larger end moment and |r_m| ≤ 1. And the sign matters: the original course spreadsheet takes r_m positive even for double curvature, which gives a limit about half the right one (Worked Example 7.1: 17.7 instead of 36.2).
Key points:
- λ_{lim} = 20ABC/√n with A = 0.7, B = 1.1 if unknown; n = N_{Ed}/(A_cf_{cd}).
- C = 1.7 − r_m: r_m negative in double curvature; r_m = 1 (C = 0.7) when unbraced or when imperfections dominate.
- λ ≤ λ_{lim}: non-slender (Unit 8). λ > λ_{lim}: slender (Unit 9). One verdict per axis.
Quick check (not graded): A braced column has end moments of 60 kN m at the top and 35 kN m at the bottom, giving tension on opposite faces. N_{Ed}l_0/400 = 9.6 kN m. What is C?
Options: 1.12 | 2.28 | 0.70 | 1.70
Explanation shown after answering: Double curvature, so r_m = −35/60 = −0.583 and C = 1.7 + 0.583 = 2.28. Taking r_m positive gives 1.12; 0.7 applies only when unbraced or when the end moments do not exceed the imperfection moment (60 > 9.6 here).

[examples-x3] Example 3 · Explain-type questions
Exam type short written answers Time ≈ 3 min each
Questions
- Explain why a column between deep beams has a shorter effective length than the same column between shallow beams.
- Explain why an unbraced column is almost always slender by EC2.
- A braced column bends in double curvature. Why is its slenderness limit higher than in single curvature?
- The analysis gives no end moments for an interior braced column. Why may you not take r_m = 0 and C = 1.7?
Write your four answers first, then open the model answers one by one.
## Answer 1 Stiff beams hold the ends
Deep beams are stiff, so they resist the rotation of the column ends: k = (I/l)_{col}/Σ2(I/l)_{beam} is small. The buckled shape then curves back near each end and the points of contraflexure move into the column, which shortens the effective length: l_0 tends to 0.5l, and to 0.59l at the floor k = 0.1. Shallow beams let the ends rotate, k grows, and l_0 tends to l (braced).
## Answer 2 Long l_0, low limit
Two effects act together. Its ends can move sideways, so l_0 ≥ l, at least 1.22l with k ≥ 0.1 (Eq. 7.3), which makes λ large: a 300 mm column with l = 3.0 m has λ ≥ 1.22 × 3000/86.6 = 42. And EC2 takes r_m = 1, C = 0.7, for unbraced members whatever the end moments, so λ_{lim} = 10.8/√n, only 11 to 15 for n between 1.0 and 0.5.
## Answer 3 An S-shape bulges less
In double curvature the end moments bend the column into an S-shape with a point of contraflexure in its height, so the sideways deflection stays small and N times that deflection adds little to the moment at the critical end. In single curvature the column bows to one side, with the largest deflection at mid-height, where the first-order moment is also large. EC2 reflects this through r_m: negative in double curvature, so C = 1.7 − r_m > 1.7 and λ_{lim} is higher.
## Answer 4 Imperfections bend it in single curvature
No column is perfectly straight or perfectly loaded: EC2 assumes an imperfection e_i = l_0/400, which bows the column to one side, so its only first-order moment is in single curvature. EC2 5.8.3.1(1) therefore takes r_m = 1 and C = 0.7. Using C = 1.7 would raise λ_{lim} by a factor of 2.4 and could pass a slender column as short.

[glossary-column] Glossary: column
column: A compression member whose section depth is at most 4 times its width and whose height is at least 3 times its depth (EC2 5.3.1(7)); otherwise it is a wall.

[glossary-braced-member] Glossary: braced member
braced member: A member assumed not to contribute to the horizontal stability of the structure: walls or cores carry the horizontal load, so its ends do not sway (EC2 5.8.1).

[glossary-bracing-member-bracing-system] Glossary: bracing member · bracing system
bracing member · bracing system: Walls, lift cores or cross-bracing that carry the horizontal load of the building and keep the frame from swaying.

[glossary-unbraced-member-sway] Glossary: unbraced member · sway
unbraced member · sway: A member of a frame that resists the horizontal load by bending, so its ends move sideways relative to each other (sway).

[glossary-non-slender-short-column] Glossary: non-slender (short) column
non-slender (short) column: A column with λ ≤ λ_{lim} about the axis considered: second-order effects may be ignored, and it fails by crushing of the section.

[glossary-slender-column] Glossary: slender column
slender column: A column with λ > λ_{lim} : the second-order moment must be added to the design moment (Unit 9).

[glossary-first-order-effects] Glossary: first-order effects
first-order effects: Action effects calculated without the deformation of the structure, but including geometric imperfections (EC2 5.8.1).

[glossary-second-order-effects-p] Glossary: second-order effects · P–Δ
second-order effects · P–Δ: Additional effects caused by the deformation of the structure: the axial load acting on the lateral deflection adds moment.

[glossary-buckling-euler-load-n-cr] Glossary: buckling · Euler load N_{cr}
buckling · Euler load N_{cr}: Failure by instability of a member under axial compression. For an elastic pin-ended member N_{cr} = π²EI/l_0 ².

[glossary-effective-length-l-0] Glossary: effective length l_0
effective length l_0: The length of a pin-ended column with the same section and the same buckling load as the real one; also called the buckling length.

[glossary-clear-height-l] Glossary: clear height l
clear height l: The height of the column between its end restraints. In this course: the storey height minus the depth of the beams in the plane considered.

[glossary-point-of-contraflexure] Glossary: point of contraflexure
point of contraflexure: A point of zero moment where the curvature changes sign. The effective length is the distance between two such points on the buckled shape.

[glossary-end-restraint] Glossary: end restraint
end restraint: The resistance to rotation at a column end given by the beams or the foundation.

[glossary-relative-flexibility-k] Glossary: relative flexibility k
relative flexibility k: k = (θ/M)(EI/l) at a column end; in this course (I/l)_{col} /Σ2(I/l)_{beam} , never below 0.1. Small k: stiff restraint.

[glossary-stiffness-k-i-l] Glossary: stiffness K = I/l
stiffness K = I/l: The relative stiffness of a member, used in k and in moment distribution; E cancels when all members have the same concrete.

[glossary-fixed-base-pinned-end] Glossary: fixed base · pinned end
fixed base · pinned end: A base fixed into a footing designed for the moment takes k_1 = 0.1 (the EC2 floor); a pinned end takes k = ∞.

[glossary-radius-of-gyration-i] Glossary: radius of gyration i
radius of gyration i: i = √(I/A) of the uncracked concrete section about the axis of bending; h/√12 = 0.289h for a rectangle, with h in the plane of bending.

[glossary-slenderness-ratio] Glossary: slenderness ratio λ
slenderness ratio λ: λ = l_0 /i, about each axis (EC2 Eq. 5.14).

[glossary-slenderness-limit-lim] Glossary: slenderness limit λ_{lim}
slenderness limit λ_{lim}: λ_{lim} = 20ABC/√n (EC2 Eq. 5.13N); below it, second-order effects may be ignored.

[glossary-relative-axial-force-n] Glossary: relative axial force n
relative axial force n: n = N_{Ed} /(A_c f_{cd} ): how hard the column is pushed compared with its concrete strength.

[glossary-moment-ratio-r-m] Glossary: moment ratio r_m
moment ratio r_m: r_m = M_{01} /M_{02} with |M_{02} | ≥ |M_{01} |; negative in double curvature; taken as 1 for unbraced columns and when imperfections dominate.

[glossary-single-curvature-double-curvature] Glossary: single curvature · double curvature
single curvature · double curvature: Single: the end moments give tension on the same face and the column bows to one side. Double: tension on opposite faces, an S-shape with a point of contraflexure.

[glossary-geometric-imperfection-e-i] Glossary: geometric imperfection e_i
geometric imperfection e_i: An assumed eccentricity for out-of-straightness and misplaced loads; e_i = l_0 /400 for isolated braced columns (EC2 5.2(9)).

[glossary-minimum-eccentricity-e-0] Glossary: minimum eccentricity e_0
minimum eccentricity e_0: e_0 = max(h/30, 20 mm): every column is designed for at least N_{Ed} e_0 (EC2 6.1(4), Unit 8).

[glossary-effective-creep-ratio-ef] Glossary: effective creep ratio φ_{ef}
effective creep ratio φ_{ef}: Creep under the quasi-permanent load, scaled by the moment ratio; it enters A = 1/(1 + 0.2φ_{ef} ), taken as 0.7 when unknown.

[glossary-mechanical-reinforcement-ratio] Glossary: mechanical reinforcement ratio ω
mechanical reinforcement ratio ω: ω = A_s f_{yd} /(A_c f_{cd} ); it enters B = √(1 + 2ω), taken as 1.1 when unknown.

[glossary-major-axis-minor-axis] Glossary: major axis · minor axis
major axis · minor axis: The stiffer and the weaker axes of a section; in the course notes z (I_z = bh³/12) and y (I_y = hb³/12).

[glossary-nominal-curvature-method] Glossary: nominal curvature method
nominal curvature method: The EC2 5.8.8 method that adds a nominal second-order moment M_2 = N_{Ed} e_2 to a slender column (Unit 9).
